title: A thousand cows for the wisest
hookLine: a king offers a thousand gold-horned cows to the wisest person in the room, and only one man dares to take them
tomorrow: Ashvala asks about death and ritual
last: ONE SELF IN ALL, SO ALL FEED EACH OTHER.

lines: A THOUSAND COWS. GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.
cards: A royal courtyard, crowded with learned priests from the Kuru and Panchala lands. In the middle, penned together, a thousand cows. On the horns of every one, the text says, gold is tied.
King Janaka stands up. Honored scholars, he says, whoever among you is wisest in Brahman, drive these cows home. The room goes silent.
Nobody moves. Taking the cows means claiming to be the wisest person there, and every other priest will come for you.

teach.b: Then Yajnavalkya turns to his own student. Samashravas, my dear, he says, drive them home. And the student does.
How can he call himself the wisest among us? The king's own hotri priest, Ashvala, steps up. Yajnavalkya, are you really the wisest among us?
And Yajnavalkya answers. We bow to the wisest.
We just want the cows. It's funny, and it's sly. He claims nothing, and he'll answer any question you've got.
That sets up the whole third book of the Brihadaranyaka: a day of debate.
One after another, challengers step forward, one of them twice, each with the hardest question they have. Over the next ten days we'll take them one at a time. And a word about the king.
Janaka of Videha appears again and again in these texts as a king hungry for teaching.
Sita's father in the Ramayana is also called Janaka, king of Videha. Nobody can say for sure whether they're the same man. Now the teaching in this scene.
In the Upanishads, knowing Brahman isn't settled by a title. It's tested in the open, question by question, and Hindu tradition kept that habit of scriptural debate, later called shastrartha.
And the one who knows doesn't announce it. The Bhagavad Gita says how to learn from the wise: by bowing, by asking questions, and by serving. So in this tradition, asking wait, why? isn't disrespect.

how: The debate in Janaka's court, the third book of the Brihadaranyaka, is studied in Vedanta as a series of short dialogues; Hindu tradition remembers Janaka as a model of the king who lives among riches without clinging to them.

s: Yajnavalkya stood up and declared himself the wisest
he never claimed it. we bow to the wisest, he said; we just want the cows.
in Hindu tradition, you learn from the wise by questioning them, not only by bowing
the Gita says learn by bowing, asking and serving, and Yajnavalkya takes every challenger's question.
it's certain that this Janaka is Sita's father in the Ramayana
both are kings of Videha called Janaka, but nobody can say for sure they're the same man.

games.q: you're Yajnavalkya. the king offers a thousand gold-horned cows to the wisest, and the whole room is silent. what do you do?
o: tell your student to drive the cows home.
give a speech proving you're the wisest.
games.why: he quietly tells his student to drive them home. when challenged, he doesn't argue: we bow to the wisest; we just want the cows.

practice: If a memory comes, recall a time you stayed quiet in a room because speaking up meant being judged: a meeting, a class, a family dinner. Don't relive it; just notice how it felt in the body.
Then bring to mind Yajnavalkya's ease, we bow to the wisest, and let some of it into your shoulders as you breathe. Your questions belong in the room.

wordCard.voice: Janaka's court. Where a king asked for the brahmishtha, the one most wise in Brahman: the title nobody there dared to claim, and Yajnavalkya never quite claimed either.

orig.note: Sanskrit brahmiṣṭha: most knowing of Brahman, the superlative Janaka used for the prize.

carryVoice: Your line: wisdom isn't claimed; it's questioned. Tomorrow, the first challenger, a priest, steps up. Day three hundred seventy-one, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.34 (learn by bowing, by questioning, by service)
